title: The Rothschilds and the Five Arrows
text:
Mayer Amschel Rothschild grew up in the crowded Jewish quarter of Frankfurt, the Judengasse, where Jews lived under harsh restrictions. Starting as a dealer in rare coins, he built a trading and banking business and became agent to the Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel.

He had five sons, and he sent them out across Europe. Amschel stayed in Frankfurt, Salomon went to Vienna, Nathan to London, Carl to Naples and James to Paris. The brothers wrote to each other constantly, often in Hebrew script, and lent money, moved gold and shared information across borders in a way no single bank could. In his will of 1812, Mayer ordered that the business stay in the hands of his sons and their male heirs, and urged them to remain united.

In 1822 the Austrian emperor made the five brothers barons. Their coat of arms showed a hand holding five arrows, one for each brother, with the motto Concordia, Integritas, Industria: unity, integrity, diligence. Family tradition connects the arrows to the ancient story, told by Plutarch, of a Scythian king who showed his sons that a bundle of arrows could not be broken although each single arrow could.

For much of the nineteenth century the Rothschild houses, working together, were the most powerful bank in the world.
lesson: A family that spreads out but keeps faith with one another can be stronger than any single member. Unity is a decision renewed by constant contact, not a feeling.
people: Mayer Amschel Rothschild, Amschel, Salomon, Nathan, Carl and James Rothschild
location: Frankfurt, Germany; Vienna; London; Naples; Paris
source: Niall Ferguson, The House of Rothschild: Money's Prophets 1798 to 1848 (1998); Rothschild Archive, coat of arms of 1822
caveat: The deathbed arrow scene sometimes told of Mayer Amschel is family legend; the arms and the will are documented.
